question.:question/problem:
If the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $1,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of ${315}^{∘}$ with the positive $x$-axis, then the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are$\,(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$, where

$$
r=1,\,\theta ={315}^{∘}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡({315}^{∘}) \\  & =1\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡({315}^{∘}) \\  & =1\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$

$$
r=5\sqrt{3},\,\theta =\frac{2π}{3}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2π}{3}) \\  & =5\sqrt{3}(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2π}{3}) \\  & =5\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{15}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{15}{2}).$
